description:
We are a team of six enthusiastic students participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are interested in programming, technology, science, and AI. Our skills include Python, web development, databases, and information systems. We are creative, motivated, and enjoy solving problems together

We are looking for teammates with skills in Python, JavaScript, data analysis, machine learning UI/UX design, or astronomy. Most importantly we value creativity, teamwork, and a willingness to learn
summary: Zuma is a local desktop prototype that helps crew members record wellbeing and review cognitive game performance during long-duration missions. Users save a survey about sleep, fatigue, stress, and mood, then play one of four short games: Fifteen Puzzle, Find the Pair, Speed Math, or Remember the Numbers. A Go server validates game events, stores results in SQLite, and produces history, trends, and printable reports with comparisons to compatible earlier attempts. A persistent local queue preserves completed attempts when delivery fails. Optional Qwen3 8B explanations run through Ollama; numerical calculations remain in Go and the core workflow works without AI or an internet connection after setup. NASA resources on spaceflight risks, sleep loss, and behavioral health informed the survey and repeated-observation workflow. Zuma makes personal observations easier to collect and revisit in a clear, engaging interface. It is an experimental prototype, not a clinically validated assessment or medical device, and does not collect wearable biometrics.
details:
PURPOSE AND CHALLENGE

Long-duration missions make reliable self-observation and locally available information important. Zuma explores a simple routine: record wellbeing, complete a short cognitive game, and review personal results over time. It addresses the software and self-reported indicators portion of the challenge, rather than physical vital-sign monitoring.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Create or select a profile and save a survey covering sleep duration, fatigue, stress, and mood.

2. Choose a game and difficulty. Fifteen Puzzle uses tile ordering; Find the Pair uses matching after a preview; Speed Math uses timed multiple-choice arithmetic; Remember the Numbers uses ordered recall of numbered positions. Layouts or questions vary between attempts.

3. The client records game events and attaches the latest saved survey snapshot. Completed attempts enter a persistent local outbox for delivery and retry.

4. The Go API validates and replays supported events, stores results in SQLite, and produces descriptive reports. History and trends group compatible games, difficulty levels, rules versions, and protocols.

5. An optional local model selects from server-generated facts to explain results. The numerical report remains available without the model.

DESIGN AND INTENDED BENEFIT

A concise English interface, instructions before play, and a reusable Godot module make repeated observations approachable. Keeping the client, storage, and model local reduces dependence on cloud connectivity. Event-based validation and explicit comparison rules make results more traceable. The intended benefit is a convenient record for reflection and discussion, not an automated diagnosis.

TECHNOLOGY

Godot 4 and GDScript provide the desktop UI and games. Go implements the HTTP API, validation, calculations, and printable HTML/JSON reports. SQLite stores profiles and results. Ollama runs optional Qwen3 8B locally. Windows packages include the application and API server; model weights are installed separately.

NASA RESOURCES

NASA Human Research Program resources on risks of spaceflight, sleep loss/circadian disruption/work overload, and behavioral health informed the choice of self-reported measures and repeated comparisons. These are contextual research resources, not a NASA clinical dataset used to train or validate the games.

IMPLEMENTATION AND VALIDATION

The prototype includes four playable games, survey drafts, offline delivery retry, history, trends, and reports. Automated checks cover the Go API, client/server integration, all 12 game/difficulty combinations, interface layout, Windows export, and the optional local-model workflow. Test fixtures are synthetic. These engineering checks do not establish medical validity.

AI DISCLOSURE

OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, debugging, tests, and documentation. Google Stitch supplied UI design references. Qwen3 8B through Ollama is an optional runtime component that selects from predefined report facts; it does not calculate scores or diagnose conditions. Synthetic test fixtures are labeled and are not astronaut observations.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

No smart watches, heart-rate sensors, HRV measurements, or other wearable biometrics are integrated. Games and measures are not clinically validated. Survey values are self-reported and a saved survey may be reused for several attempts. Local storage is not encrypted. Further work requires usability evaluation, security hardening, and expert-led validation before any operational or medical use.
